title: The Cider Merchant's Son: Beaumont-en-Auge, the Ecole Militaire, and the System of the World
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Beaumont-en-Auge, the birth of the syndic's son
stops.date_confidence: Date attested by the MacTutor biography and by en.wikipedia. Coordinates 49.2789, 0.1106 from fr.wikipedia 'Beaumont-en-Auge' (49 deg 16 min 44 sec N, 0 deg 06 min 38 sec E). The research pool's geography lens carried 49.3097, 0.1167, some 3.5 km north of the village and out toward the Touques valley, while its own afterlife lens used the village value; the contradiction is resolved in favour of the commune article and the village value is used throughout this file.
stops.campa: In a small town of the Pays d'Auge, above the valley of the Touques, a son is born to Pierre Laplace, cider trader and syndic of the parish, and to Marie-Anne Sochon. The family is neither noble nor poor. It holds land, it holds a parish office, and it intends the boy for the Church, which is what a comfortable Norman household does with a clever second son. Normandy in 1749 sends such boys to Caen and then to a benefice. Nothing in the parish register marks him out. He is baptized Pierre-Simon.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of Beaumont-en-Auge, Calvados, for March 1749

stops.name: Beaumont-en-Auge, the Benedictine priory school
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the schooling, [R] for the span. MacTutor states that he attended the priory school from about the age of seven to the age of sixteen, i.e. c.1756-1765, and the Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 12(2) (2009), p. 93, agrees that he remained at the college of Beaumont-en-Auge until he reached sixteen. The research pool's chronology lens dated the schooling to 1765, which is the year he left it and not the year he entered. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The priory's foundation in 1060 by Robert Bertran de Roncheville, its dependence on Saint-Ouen of Rouen, and its church of Saint-Sauveur now serving as the parish church are from fr.wikipedia 'Beaumont-en-Auge'.
stops.campa: The priory dates from 1060, a foundation of the vicomte Robert Bertran de Roncheville, and depends on the abbey of Saint-Ouen at Rouen; its church of Saint-Sauveur is the church of the town. The school attached to it takes him at about seven and keeps him nine years, and an uncle of his teaches in it. No mathematics is taught. What he learns is the trivium: Latin, rhetoric, and the arguing of a thesis down to its conclusion, and what he is known for in Normandy at sixteen is theology and a gift for disputation.
suggested_refs: The priory church of Saint-Sauveur, Beaumont-en-Auge, founded 1060, now the parish church
sources: Montgomery, Orchiston and Whittingham, 'Michell, Laplace and the Origin of the Black Hole Concept', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 12(2) (2009), p. 93

stops.name: Caen, the university and the two mathematicians
stops.date_confidence: Attested by MacTutor and fr.wikipedia: he entered the University of Caen at sixteen, formally to read theology, and the mathematics teachers Christophe Gadbled and Pierre Le Canu turned him toward analysis. Month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates 49.1817, -0.3728 are the corpus-canonical Caen pin, the pair used most often in the existing files; the research pool gave 49.1857, -0.3707 for the same city, a difference of about 500 metres.
stops.campa: He enters the University of Caen at sixteen, matriculated for the Church. Inside the arts faculty two men teach mathematics, Christophe Gadbled and Pierre Le Canu, and they put analysis in front of him. He does not go back. Within two years the theology is a formality he has stopped attending to and the thing he is actually doing is a memoir on the principles of mechanics. Caen has no chair worth holding and no journal worth printing in. So he writes to Turin, and he writes to Paris.
suggested_refs: Christophe Gadbled and Pierre Le Canu, mathematics teachers in the arts faculty at Caen in the 1760s

stops.name: Caen, leaving without a degree
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests that he left Caen without taking a degree and travelled to Paris at about nineteen or twenty carrying letters of introduction. The research pool's chronology lens dates the Paris journey to 1768; no month is fixed by any source reached, and the day is defaulted. Coordinates as at the previous stop.
stops.campa: He walks out of the university with no degree at all. For a young man intended for a benefice this is the closing of one career and the opening of nothing whatever. Behind him is a household that expected a priest; ahead is a city where he knows no one and has no income. What he takes with him is a packet of letters of introduction to men who have never heard of him, and a memoir on the general principles of mechanics in his own hand. He is nineteen or twenty; the year is 1768.
suggested_refs: The matriculation and degree registers of the University of Caen, 1765-1768, not consulted

stops.name: Paris, the letter to d'Alembert
stops.date_confidence: [R]. MacTutor and en.wikipedia agree that Laplace arrived in Paris with letters of introduction to Jean le Rond d'Alembert, that d'Alembert was unmoved by the recommendations, and that he was won over by a memoir on mechanics sent unasked, after which he found the young man a teaching post. The scene of the successive letters and d'Alembert's reply is biographical tradition; no letter is cited by any source reached, and the wording attributed to d'Alembert is not quoted as a quotation here. Generic central-Paris pin 48.8566, 2.3522 inherited from alexis_de_tocqueville.journey.json by way of augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json, for a stop with no fixed address. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Jean le Rond d'Alembert receives letters of recommendation on behalf of a nineteen-year-old Norman and does nothing about them; the men recommending are men he does not know. Laplace sends instead a memoir on the general principles of mechanics, written for one reader. D'Alembert reads it and answers at once. The tradition has him say that he paid little enough attention to recommendations, and that this young man has no need of any. Within a year he has found him a salary.
suggested_refs: The lost memoir on the general principles of mechanics sent to d'Alembert, 1768 or 1769

stops.name: Ecole Militaire, Paris: the chair of mathematics
stops.date_confidence: The appointment on d'Alembert's recommendation is attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia; the 1769-1776 span is confirmed by Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 12(2) (2009), p. 93. Month not recorded, defaulted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from captain_alfred_dreyfus.journey.json (48.8525, 2.3036), whose date_confidence records the correction to en.wikipedia's 48 deg 51 min 09 sec N, 2 deg 18 min 13 sec E; napoleon.journey.json carries 48.8557, 2.3055 for the same building and the difference is not resolved here. The research pool's geography lens gave 48.8553, 2.3057, which lands on the Champ de Mars north of the building.
stops.campa: D'Alembert gets him the mathematics of the Ecole Militaire, where the sons of poor provincial nobles are drilled into artillery and engineer officers. He teaches them the geometry and the trigonometry a gunner needs, and the school keeps him until 1776. The post pays, and it puts a twenty-year-old with no degree inside the military school system of the kingdom. He does his own work at night, after the cadets have gone. He holds the chair for seven years.
suggested_refs: The teaching registers of the Ecole Militaire, Paris, 1769-1776
sources: Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 12(2) (2009), p. 93

stops.name: Academie royale des sciences, the Louvre: the first paper
stops.date_confidence: Date attested by MacTutor, which also records thirteen papers submitted in under three years and two failed candidacies before election. Louvre pin 48.8606, 2.3376 is corpus-canonical: gottfried_wilhelm_leibniz.journey.json uses it for the Academy's Louvre quarters, and al_ghafiqi.journey.json and frida_kahlo.journey.json for the Louvre itself.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of March he reads a paper on maxima and minima to the Academy. He is twenty-one, a provincial nobody with a teaching post at a military school. Over the next three years he lays thirteen memoirs on this table, on difference equations, on integral calculus, on the motions of the planets, at a rate the secretaries find hard to keep pace with. Twice in that stretch the Academy puts up somebody else at election, in 1771 and again in 1772. The memoirs keep arriving at the same rate through both refusals.
suggested_refs: The proces-verbaux of the Academie royale des sciences for 1770-1773, not consulted

stops.name: Turin, the paper in the Miscellanea
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia attests a first paper on integral calculus and finite differences published in the Turin academy's Miscellanea, and states that it opened his correspondence with Joseph-Louis Lagrange. The paper was written in France; the stop is pinned at the place of publication and of the correspondent, and this is a decision, not a source claim. Month not recorded. Turin pin 45.0703, 7.6869 is the corpus-canonical pair. Lagrange has no journey file in the corpus at the time of writing; he stands in QUEUE.md.
stops.campa: The Turin academy prints a paper of his on integral calculus and finite differences. Turin is where Joseph-Louis Lagrange, thirteen years his elder and already the finest analyst alive, edits and publishes. From this volume the two men begin to write to each other and do not stop for fifty years: comparators, rivals, at last colleagues on the same committees in the same city, each of them the only reader in Europe capable of following the other at speed. He is twenty-two when the volume appears.
suggested_refs: Miscellanea Taurinensia / Melanges de Turin, the volumes edited by Lagrange in the 1770s
QUEUE.md, row for Joseph-Louis Lagrange

stops.name: Academie royale des sciences, the Louvre: elected adjoint
stops.date_confidence: Date attested by MacTutor, as are the two earlier failed candidacies of 1771 and 1772. The Lexell remark is quoted on the MacTutor page and dated there to c.1780-1781; the original Lexell text was not consulted, and the wording is therefore provisional.
stops.campa: At the third attempt, after failing in 1771 and again in 1772, he is elected adjoint at twenty-four. Thirteen memoirs in under three years have made a third refusal harder to arrange than an election. He is the youngest man taken into the section in years, and the men who voted for him begin at once to complain about his manner in the room. Anders Johan Lexell, over from Petersburg a few years later and sitting through the sessions in the Louvre quarters, writes down what they say.
stops.quote: in the Academy he wanted to pronounce on everything.
stops.quote_source: Anders Johan Lexell on Laplace's conduct at the Academie royale des sciences, c.1780-1781, as quoted in the MacTutor biography (mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk); the original Lexell text was not consulted.
suggested_refs: The election registers of the Academie royale des sciences, 31 March 1773

stops.name: Paris, the great inequality of Jupiter and Saturn
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the beginning of the research programme on the long-term invariability of the planetary mean motions to 1773, without a month; 06-01 is a placed value used only to order this stop after the March election and is not a source date. The near five to two resonance of Jupiter and Saturn and the resulting great inequality are attested by the same source. Generic Paris pin as above, the work having no single address.
stops.campa: Jupiter appears to be speeding up and Saturn to be slowing down, and has done for as long as anyone has kept records. Newton thought a system of this kind would need occasional repair from outside. Laplace takes the two planets whose periods stand near a ratio of five to two and shows that the drift is an oscillation on a scale of centuries and not a decay, and that the mean motions of the planets are invariable. He begins this at twenty-four and it takes the rest of his working life.
stops.quote: All events, even those which on account of their insignificance do not seem to follow the great laws of nature, are a result of it just as necessarily as the revolutions of the sun.
stops.quote_source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, Truscott and Emory translation (1902), Chapter II, verbatim; the sentence immediately precedes the 'intelligence' passage. Written forty years after this stop and quoted for the doctrine the stability work is the first instalment of, not as a document of 1773.
suggested_refs: The Jupiter-Saturn great inequality and the 5:2 near-resonance
Newton's Opticks, Query 31, on the need for periodic divine correction of the system

stops.name: Paris, the probability of causes
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia attests that the Memoire sur la probabilite des causes par les evenements was read to the Academy in 1773 and published in 1774, and dates the derivation of the double-exponential error law now called the Laplace distribution to 1774. The stop is dated to publication because the month of the reading is not recorded. Generic Paris pin as above.
stops.campa: The Memoire sur la probabilite des causes par les evenements gives a rule for running inference backward: given what has happened, what were the odds on the thing that produced it. The heavens are a mechanism whose future is already fixed, and the observer is a creature of partial information who has to bet; in his hands the two problems are one problem, and he does not separate them again. In the same year he derives the double-exponential error law that still carries his name. He is twenty-five.
stops.quote: Present events are connected with preceding ones by a tie based upon the evident principle that a thing cannot occur without a cause which produces it.
stops.quote_source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, Truscott and Emory translation (1902), Chapter II, 'Concerning Probability'. Written forty years later than this stop and quoted here for the principle, not as a document of 1774.
suggested_refs: Memoire sur la probabilite des causes par les evenements (read 1773, published 1774)
The Laplace distribution, derived 1774

stops.name: Paris, the ice calorimeter with Lavoisier
stops.date_confidence: The collaboration with Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier, the ice-calorimeter measurements, and the joint Memoire sur la chaleur are attested by en.wikipedia and dated 1783; the research pool's geography lens gives the working span as 1782-1784. Month not recorded. Haüy's printed thanks to Laplace, beside Daubenton and Bezout, appear in the Discours preliminaire of his Essai d'une theorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784) and reach this file through rene_hauy.journey.json; the teaching itself is undated in every source reached. Generic Paris pin, the laboratory address not being fixed by any source here.
stops.campa: With Antoine Lavoisier he builds an apparatus of nested ice: a living animal in the inner chamber, meltwater collected from the outer, the warmth of a body measured as the weight of water that runs out of it. The joint memoir on heat ties animal warmth to combustion. Eleven years from now Lavoisier will be guillotined and Laplace will not. In the same Paris years the abbe Rene Just Hauy prints his thanks to Laplace, beside Daubenton and Bezout, for the geometry that let his crystals be described.
suggested_refs: Lavoisier and Laplace, Memoire sur la chaleur (1783)
rene_hauy.journey.json, for the thanks printed in the Discours preliminaire of the Essai (1784)

stops.date_confidence: [R]. No examination register has been cited by any source reached, and the [R] tag rests on that absence rather than on doubt that the two men were in the room. Day not recorded, defaulted. Coordinates as at the 1769 stop, and differing from napoleon.journey.json's 48.8557, 2.3055 for the same event at the same building.
stops.campa: He is made an examiner of the Royal Artillery Corps, which means that no boy becomes a gunner in France without passing through his questions. In September a sixteen-year-old Corsican sits the graduation examination at the Ecole Militaire, is passed, and is commissioned into the artillery. Napoleon Bonaparte will remember it. Fourteen years later he will make his examiner Minister of the Interior of France, and six weeks after that he will take the ministry back off him.

stops.name: Eglise Saint-Sulpice, Paris: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged and not resolved: en.wikipedia gives 15 March 1788, MacTutor gives 15 May 1788. The research pool's geography lens reversed this attribution while its chronology lens had it right; the en.wikipedia date is used for the stop and the MacTutor date is recorded here. en.wikipedia gives the bride's age as eighteen and her origin as Besancon, while the pool elsewhere says only that she was about half his age. The son Charles-Emile-Pierre-Joseph was born 5 April 1789 and the daughter Sophie-Suzanne in 1792 (en.wikipedia); the son's later career as artillery officer, lieutenant-general, hereditary marquis and senator under Napoleon III, dying childless, is from the same source. Saint-Sulpice pin 48.8514, 2.3342 from the corpus; the church stands at about 48.8511, 2.3348.
stops.campa: At thirty-eight he marries Marie-Anne-Charlotte de Courty de Romanges, eighteen years old, of Besancon, at Saint-Sulpice. A son, Charles-Emile, follows in April of the next year, three months before the Bastille. A daughter, Sophie-Suzanne, follows in 1792 and will die at twenty-one. The son will be an artillery officer, then a lieutenant-general, then a hereditary marquis and a senator under a third Napoleon, and will die without children, so that the line ends in him.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of Saint-Sulpice, Paris, March or May 1788, not consulted

stops.name: Paris, the commission on weights and measures
stops.date_confidence: Laplace's service on the revolutionary commission standardizing weights and measures, and his removal from it by the Committee of Public Safety in December 1793 on the stated ground that the work required men of stronger republican confidence, are attested by MacTutor and fr.wikipedia. The 1790 start is the research pool's geography lens, which gives the span as 1790-1793; no month is recorded and the day is defaulted. The names of the others struck off at the same time are from the standard accounts of the commission and were not verified against a primary list; treat that clause as [R].
stops.campa: The Assembly appoints a commission to fix the measures of France by nature instead of by custom, and Laplace sits on it with Lagrange, Borda, Monge and Condorcet. The metre is to be a fraction of the meridian, the kilogram a volume of water, the whole apparatus decimal, universal, and owned by nobody. In December 1793 the Committee of Public Safety strikes him from the list, on the ground that the work requires men whose republican convictions are less open to doubt. No charge is laid and no arrest is made. The commission goes on without him.
suggested_refs: The Commission des poids et mesures and the meridian survey of Delambre and Mechain
The arrete of the Committee of Public Safety, December 1793, not consulted in the original

stops.name: Melun, out of reach
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests that during the most violent phase of the Terror he settled some fifty kilometres southeast of Paris and returned after Robespierre's fall in July 1794, and that unlike Lavoisier he was never arrested. Lavoisier was guillotined on 8 May 1794. The month of the removal is not recorded and the date is defaulted. Coordinates 48.5396, 2.6598 are the research pool's value for Melun; the corpus carries two other Melun pairs, 48.535 / 2.6607 and 48.5421 / 2.6622, and the spread of about 400 metres is not resolved here.
stops.campa: He moves his household fifty kilometres southeast of Paris and stays there while the Academy is abolished and his collaborator on the calorimeter is tried in a morning and beheaded in an afternoon. Melun is a day's ride from the capital, near enough to hear what is happening and far enough not to be seen not doing anything about it. Laplace is not arrested, not denounced, not charged with anything. He comes back after Thermidor and resumes. Nothing in the record says what he thought of the year, and he never afterwards put a line on paper about it.
suggested_refs: The suppression of the Academie royale des sciences, August 1793
The trial and execution of Lavoisier, 8 May 1794

stops.name: Jardin des Plantes, Paris: the Ecole normale de l'an III
stops.date_confidence: Opening date attested by fr.wikipedia 'Ecole normale de l'an III': the school ran from 20 January to 19 May 1795 and its lectures were held in an amphitheatre of the Museum national d'histoire naturelle at the Jardin des Plantes. Laplace shared the chair of mathematics with Lagrange; the research pool's geography lens described him as teaching probability, which is a strand of those lectures rather than the chair, and pinned the stop at 48.8462, 2.3372, up by the Pantheon and nearer the later rue d'Ulm school founded in 1808. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from joseph_fourier.journey.json (48.8416, 2.3622), whose 1795-01-20 stop pins the same amphitheatre; the interlock lens reported that pin as 48.8443, 2.3622, which the file itself does not bear out. Fourier's attendance is attested there from MacTutor.
stops.campa: The Republic gathers provincial schoolmasters into an amphitheatre at the Jardin des Plantes and has the best men in France lecture at them for four months. Laplace shares the mathematics with Lagrange, and the introduction he writes for those lectures is the seed of everything he will later publish for general readers. On the benches sits Joseph Fourier, twenty-six, a schoolmaster lately out of a prison cell and twelve years from the committee that will refuse his memoir on heat. The school closes on the nineteenth of May.
suggested_refs: joseph_fourier.journey.json, stop 'Paris, the Ecole normale de l'an III'

stops.name: Petit Luxembourg, Paris: the Bureau des Longitudes
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia 'Bureau des longitudes': the body was created by the law of 25 June 1795 (7 messidor an III) and held its first meeting on 6 July 1795 in a room of the Petit Luxembourg, with Laplace a founding member as geometre alongside Lagrange, Mechain, Cassini and Delambre. The research pool's geography lens placed the founding at the Institut de France, which the same article contradicts, and separately asserted that the Paris Observatory was the Bureau's institutional seat, which it also contradicts: the Observatory was placed under the Bureau's oversight from 1795 to 1854. Coordinates 48.8489, 2.3369 for the Petit Luxembourg are not a corpus-canonical pin and are taken from the building's position.
stops.campa: A law of messidor creates one body to hold the astronomy, the navigation, the geodesy and the timekeeping of the Republic, and on the sixth of July it sits for the first time in a room of the Petit Luxembourg. Laplace is a founding geometer, with Lagrange, Mechain, Cassini and Delambre. He has never taken an observation in his life and will run French astronomy through this committee until he dies. From this year until 1854 the Paris Observatory answers to it.
suggested_refs: The law of 7 messidor an III creating the Bureau des longitudes
The proces-verbaux of the Bureau des longitudes, first session, 6 July 1795

stops.name: Paris, the Exposition du systeme du monde
stops.date_confidence: Publication in 1796 attested by en.wikipedia, with the nebular hypothesis in the final book; month not recorded. The dark-star passage and the separate 1799 mathematical proof, published in German in Allgemeine Geographische Ephemeriden vol. 4, are documented by Montgomery, Orchiston and Whittingham, Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 12(2) (2009), 90-96, which also traces the modern rediscovery of the Michell-Laplace dark star to Schaffer, 'John Michell and black holes', Journal for the History of Astronomy 10 (1979), 42-43, with Israel 1987 as the elaboration; the research pool's afterlife lens credited the rediscovery to Israel and that is corrected here. Immanuel Kant published an anonymous rotating-cloud cosmogony in 1755; Laplace is not recorded as having read it, the two men never met or corresponded, and the connection is therefore carried in the refs and not named in the prose.
stops.campa: He writes the system of the world out in words, without a single equation, for readers who will never open the Mecanique celeste. The last book of it proposes that the sun once had an atmosphere which contracted, spun faster, and shed rings that condensed into the planets. In the same work he argues that a star of sufficient mass and density would hold its own light back and be invisible from outside. A mathematical proof of it follows in 1799, printed in German. Nobody takes the dark bodies seriously for a hundred and eighty years.
stops.quote: If man had confined himself to collecting facts alone, science would only have presented a steril nomenclature, and he would never have attained the knowledge of the great laws of nature.
stops.quote_source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, The System of the World, tr. J. Pond (1809), vol. 1, p. 205, at the head of Book II, 'On the real Motions of the Heavenly Bodies'; verified on archive.org, systemworld01laplgoog. The French of the Exposition reads 'Si l'homme s'etait borne a recueillir des faits, les sciences ne seraient qu'une nomenclature sterile...'. The research pool attributed this sentence to the Essai philosophique sur les probabilites, where the word nomenclature does not occur at all; the misattribution is corrected here.
suggested_refs: Exposition du systeme du monde (1796), Book V, the nebular hypothesis
Montgomery, Orchiston and Whittingham, 'Michell, Laplace and the Origin of the Black Hole Concept', JAHH 12(2) (2009), 90-96
Schaffer, 'John Michell and black holes', JHA 10 (1979), 42-43

stops.name: Paris, the first volumes of the Mecanique celeste
stops.date_confidence: Volumes I and II both appeared in 1799, per en.wikipedia's volume list for the Mecanique celeste (1799, 1799, 1802, 1805, 1825). The research pool's chronology lens dated volumes III and IV jointly to 1805, which that list contradicts. Month not recorded. The complaint about the phrase 'il est aise a voir' is a commonplace of the biographical literature rather than a documented remark by any named reader, and is offered as such.
stops.campa: The first two volumes of the Traite de mecanique celeste appear, and Newton's geometry is gone out of the subject. What replaces it is analysis: the gravitational potential, the perturbation expansions, the tides and the figure of the earth. The notation is so compressed that readers will complain for a century about the phrase it is easy to see, which is where the author has left out a page of algebra. The book carries Newtonian mechanics into the nineteenth century. Very few people can read it.
suggested_refs: Traite de mecanique celeste, vols I and II (Paris, 1799)

stops.name: Paris, Minister of the Interior
stops.date_confidence: Appointment on 12 November 1799, six days after the coup of 18 Brumaire, and removal on 25 December 1799 in favour of Lucien Bonaparte, attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia. The research pool's geography lens attached this to the Palais du Luxembourg, which housed the Senate and not the Ministry of the Interior; the ministry is deliberately left unlocated here and the generic Paris pin used instead. Napoleon's remark survives through the Memorial de Sainte-Helene of Las Cases as quoted on the MacTutor page; the Memorial itself was not consulted and the wording is provisional.
stops.campa: Six days after Brumaire the First Consul makes his old examiner Minister of the Interior of France, with the departments, the prefects, the roads, the hospitals and the census under him. It lasts six weeks. Laplace administers as he does mathematics, which is to say he pursues every particular to the bottom and settles nothing, and on Christmas Day he is replaced by the First Consul's own brother. The verdict Napoleon dictates years afterwards on Saint Helena is the sentence the ministry is remembered by.
stops.quote: because he brought the spirit of the infinitely small into the government.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon Bonaparte on Laplace's ministry, recorded in the Memorial de Sainte-Helene (Las Cases) and quoted in the MacTutor biography (mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk); the Memorial was not consulted directly and the exact wording is provisional.

stops.name: Palais du Luxembourg, Paris: the Senat conservateur
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia attests that Napoleon placed him in the Senat conservateur on 25 December 1799, immediately on his leaving the ministry. Coordinates 48.8483, 2.3372 for the Palais du Luxembourg are the corpus pair; the research pool's lens gave 48.8484, 2.3367 for the same building, a difference under sixty metres, and that discrepancy is noted rather than adopted.
stops.campa: The same day he loses the ministry he is put into the Senate, which pays well and asks nothing of him. Napoleon has learned in six weeks that the greatest mathematician in Europe cannot run a department, and has decided to keep him anyway, as an ornament and as a reliable vote. He will hold the seat through the whole Empire, use it in 1814 to help depose the man who gave it to him, and be made a peer of France five months after that by the returning king. He takes it on Christmas Day.

stops.name: Paris Observatory, the geometer at the head of the observatory
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the placement in 1800: what is attested is a span, not an event. fr.wikipedia 'Bureau des longitudes' records that the Paris Observatory was placed under the Bureau's oversight from 1795 to 1854; the research pool's geography lens stated the reverse, that the Observatory was the Bureau's institutional seat, and that justification is dropped here while the influence claim stands. He has never spent a night at an eyepiece. What he wants from the building is numbers accurate enough to feed the expansions, and the astronomers can tell. Jean-Baptiste Delambre measured the meridian arc that fixed the metre and will run the observatory himself; his objection is not about mathematics but about what an observatory is for, and he puts it in one sentence that circulates in Paris for thirty years.
stops.quote: never should one put a geometer at the head of an observatory; he will neglect all the observations except those needed for his formulas.
stops.quote_source: Jean-Baptiste Delambre on Laplace as an administrator of the Paris Observatory, quoted in the MacTutor biography (mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk); the original Delambre text was not consulted.

The author is made chevalier of the Legion of Honour on the nineteenth of vendemiaire of the year XII, and grand officier on the twenty-fifth of prairial of the same year, eight months later.

stops.name: Chateau de Malmaison, the chain of natural causes
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the conversation, [R] for the famous wording. William Herschel's Paris diary for 8 August 1802, printed in Constance A. Lubbock, The Herschel Chronicle (1933), p. 310, records Napoleon asking who is the author of all this and Laplace arguing that a chain of natural causes would account for the construction and preservation of the wonderful system; Lagrange was present too. The diary contains no 'I had no need of that hypothesis'. That sentence is traced to W. W. Rouse Ball, A Short Account of the History of Mathematics, ch. XVIII, pp. 417-418, verified on archive.org (ashortaccounthi01ballgoog) and carrying no 'Sire'. Herve Faye, Sur l'origine du monde (1884), pp. 109-111, states flatly that Laplace never said it and reports through Arago that Laplace tried to have the story suppressed. Lubbock was reached only through a citing source; archive.org returned 503 on every Herschel volume tried. Coordinates 48.8708, 2.1669 inherited byte-identical from empress_josephine.journey.json; the pool's geography lens gave 48.8797, 2.19, about two kilometres off the estate.
stops.campa: At Malmaison the First Consul, in company and looking at the extent of the sidereal heavens, exclaims and asks who is the author of all this. Herschel is standing there and writes it down that night. Laplace answers that a chain of natural causes would account for the construction and preservation of the system, and Napoleon argues with him at length. That is the whole of the eyewitness record. The sentence the world remembers, that he had no need of that hypothesis, appears in print three generations later, and Arago said Laplace had tried to have the story suppressed while he lived.
stops.quote: In ignorance of the ties which unite such events to the entire system of the universe, they have been made to depend upon final causes or upon hazard.
stops.quote_source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, Truscott and Emory translation (1902), Chapter II, verbatim. Written twelve years after this stop; it is Laplace's account of why final causes get invoked at all, and it is not a statement about God, nor a record of anything said at Malmaison.

stops.campa: South of Paris, in a village on the Bievre, Laplace buys the house next to Claude-Louis Berthollet's, and the two of them turn their gardens into an institution. On Sundays the younger men come out from the city: Biot, Poisson, Malus, Thenard, Gay-Lussac, Arago, and Alexander von Humboldt, back from four years in the Americas and not yet forty. There is no charter and no budget, only a table in a garden and two men who between them decide whose work gets read at the Institute. The Sundays run until Berthollet dies in 1822.

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the committee on Fourier's heat memoir

stops.campa: Fourier reads his memoir on the propagation of heat to the Institute on the twenty-first of December, and it goes to a committee of four: Lagrange, Laplace, Monge, Lacroix. Lagrange and Laplace will not accept the trigonometric series. The objection is not stupid, either; the convergence Fourier is assuming is not proved and will not be proved for decades. Laplace had lectured to this man in an amphitheatre at the Jardin des Plantes thirteen years before. The memoir stays unpublished.

stops.name: Paris, comte de l'Empire
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged and not resolved: fr.wikipedia dates the countship to 24 April 1808, en.wikipedia gives 1806 for the same title. The Gauss episode is attested through gauss.journey.json's 1807 stop: during the French occupation of Brunswick a war levy of 2000 francs was laid on Gauss, and both Olbers and Laplace independently offered to pay it, and Gauss refused both. gauss.journey.json also carries, at second hand from a nineteenth-century biographical dictionary by way of Wikiquote, Laplace's ranking of Gauss above Pfaff as the greatest mathematician in Europe; that ranking is therefore [R], and its date is not fixed.
stops.campa: Napoleon makes him comte de l'Empire. The year before, when a French war levy of two thousand francs was laid on Carl Friedrich Gauss at Brunswick, Laplace had written offering to pay it out of his own pocket, and Olbers had offered the same. Laplace is on record at second hand ranking Gauss above Pfaff, who examined his doctorate, as the first mathematician in Europe. He is also by now the chief ornament of the regime that was occupying Brunswick when the levy was laid. Gauss refused them both.

stops.name: Paris, the Theorie analytique des probabilites
stops.date_confidence: Publication in 1812 and the dedication to Napoleon-le-Grand are attested by MacTutor. Month not recorded, defaulted. The removal of the dedication from later printings is a commonplace of the literature and was not verified against the second and third editions; treat that sentence as [R].
stops.campa: The Theorie analytique des probabilites gathers thirty-eight years of work on chance into one system: generating functions, the limit theorem for large numbers of observations, least squares, the theory of errors, the odds on a witness telling the truth and on a court returning the right verdict. Chance, he insists throughout, is a name for ignorance and not a property of the world. The book is dedicated to Napoleon-le-Grand, and within two years the dedicatee is on Elba and the dedication is dropped from the printings that follow. The definition it starts from is a fraction.
stops.quote: The ratio of this number to that of all the cases possible is the measure of this probability, which is thus simply a fraction whose numerator is the number of favorable cases and whose denominator is the number of all the cases possible.
stops.quote_source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, Truscott and Emory translation (1902), Chapter II, pp. 6-7; the classical definition of probability. The research pool had misquoted the opening as 'The ratio of the number of favorable cases', which is a gloss; the verbatim text reads 'this number', referring back to the preceding sentence. Quoted here from the 1814 companion essay, not from the 1812 treatise.
suggested_refs: Theorie analytique des probabilites (Paris, 1812), dedicated to Napoleon-le-Grand

stops.name: Paris, the death of Sophie-Suzanne
stops.date_confidence: [R]. en.wikipedia gives the death of the daughter following childbirth on 22 September 1813 and calls it the major documented private catastrophe of his later life; the research pool tagged it R and no further source was reached. That the child survived is stated in the same source. The absence of any surviving letter or private record from Laplace about it is an honest gap and not an argument.
stops.campa: His daughter Sophie-Suzanne dies following childbirth on the twenty-second of September, twenty-one years old. The child lives. Laplace is sixty-four, a count of the Empire, in the year between his two great books on probability, and the sources that record everything else about him record of this a date and almost nothing more: no letter, no dedication, no line in the memoirs of the men who saw him every Sunday at Arcueil. He publishes the philosophical essay the following year. The family papers that might have held the rest burned in 1925.
suggested_refs: The Laplace family papers, burned with the Chateau de Mailloc in 1925

stops.name: Paris, the Essai philosophique sur les probabilites
stops.date_confidence: Publication in 1814 attested by MacTutor; the text is expanded from the introduction to the second edition of the Theorie analytique and rooted in the 1795 Ecole normale lectures. Month not recorded. The quotation is verbatim from the 1902 Truscott and Emory translation, Chapter II, verified on archive.org (philosophicaless00lapl) and on Wikisource; the em dashes in it are the translator's and the field is left untouched. The word demon appears nowhere in Laplace's text and is a later coinage.
stops.campa: He writes the probability out again in words, for readers, and in the second chapter he puts the whole of his physics into one sentence about an intelligence able to hold every force and every position at once. The sentence acquires a name in the next century, Laplace's demon, and the name is not his; he wrote intelligence, and he wrote it as a limit that nothing reaches. What it measures is the distance between what such a mind would know and what a man at a desk in Paris in 1814 can know. The word demon appears nowhere in the text.
stops.quote: Given for one instant an intelligence which could comprehend all the forces by which nature is animated and the respective situation of the beings who compose it—an intelligence sufficiently vast to submit these data to analysis—it would embrace in the same formula the movements of the greatest bodies of the universe and those of the lightest atom; for it, nothing would be uncertain and the future, as the past, would be present to its eyes.
stops.quote_source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, Truscott and Emory translation (1902), Chapter II, 'Concerning Probability'; verified against archive.org philosophicaless00lapl and Wikisource. Laplace never used the word 'demon'.
suggested_refs: Essai philosophique sur les probabilites (Paris, 1814)
en.wikisource.org, 'A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities/Chapter 2'

stops.name: Palais du Luxembourg, Paris: the vote against the Emperor

The day of the deposition vote is not recorded by any source reached and is defaulted to 01. Coordinates as at the 1799 Senate stop.
stops.campa: The allies are in Paris and the Senate is asked to depose the Emperor. Laplace votes for it. Napoleon examined him at the Ecole Militaire, made him a minister, unmade him six weeks later, seated him in this chamber and took his dedication on the great treatise on probability. A king, a republic, a consul and an emperor have each in turn distinguished him, and none of it has altered how he spends his mornings. On the fourth of June the returning Louis XVIII makes him a peer of France.

stops.name: Outside Paris, the Hundred Days
stops.date_confidence: [R]. MacTutor states that he withdrew from Paris during the Hundred Days rather than side with the restored imperial regime. No location is given by any source reached and no date; the stop is pinned at the generic Paris pin because the place of retirement is unknown, which is a compromise and not a claim, and is dated to Napoleon's entry into the Tuileries purely to order the segment. That he did not sign the Acte additionnel is inference from the same absence and is not separately attested.
stops.campa: Napoleon lands at Golfe-Juan on the first of March and is in the Tuileries within three weeks, and every man who voted in 1814 to depose him has to decide something in a hurry. Laplace leaves the city. Where he goes is not recorded anywhere reachable: no house, no town, no dated letter, only the fact of the absence. He does not sit in the imperial chamber and he does not publish. After Waterloo he comes back, and the Bourbons take him back. Whether he was ever asked to sign the Acte additionnel is not known.

stops.name: Palais du Luxembourg, Paris: the vote for Ney's death
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia attests that as a peer of France he voted for the death sentence in the trial of Marshal Michel Ney before the Chamber of Peers in December 1815. The research pool's geography lens called it a court-martial, which reverses the historical point: Ney was tried by the Chamber precisely because he had escaped trial by court-martial, and the correction is adopted. The verdict was returned on 6 December 1815 and the execution followed on 7 December; the pool gives only the month, and the two dates here are from the standard accounts of the trial.
stops.campa: Michel Ney, marshal of the Empire, the bravest of the brave, the rearguard of the retreat from Moscow, is tried by the Chamber of Peers because a court-martial would not have him. The peers vote on the sixth of December and Laplace votes for death, one of the majority that condemns him. Ney is shot near the gardens of the Luxembourg the next morning, a few hundred paces from the room in which the vote was taken. Laplace has been a peer for eighteen months. He is sixty-six.
suggested_refs: The trial of Marshal Ney before the Chamber of Peers, November-December 1815

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the Academie francaise

stops.campa: The Academie francaise elects him on the eleventh of April, so that the man who wrote the least readable book in France now sits among the forty charged with guarding its language. He has accumulated, out of regimes that exiled and shot each other's servants, every distinction the French state can hand a private man: comte under the Empire, peer under the Bourbons, a chair in each of the two academies. The following year Louis XVIII makes him marquis, and the title passes to his son.

stops.name: Institut de France, Paris: the fifth and last volume
stops.date_confidence: Volume V dated 1825 by en.wikipedia's volume list. Month not recorded. Nathaniel Bowditch's English translation with commentary of the first four volumes was substantially finished in manuscript by 1818 but delayed by publication costs and appeared from 1829, after Laplace's death; it is therefore named in the refs and not staged as an event in this file. The Rev. H. Harte's Dublin translation of the Exposition (1830) is in the same position.
stops.campa: Twenty-six years after the first two volumes the fifth appears and the Traite de mecanique celeste is finished: five quarto volumes, taking every result of a century of work on the perturbations of the solar system and rewriting the whole of it in one analytic language. Almost nobody in France reads the whole thing through, and the standard route into it for the next hundred years will not be the French text at all. He is seventy-six. The project he began at twenty-four, when he first took up Jupiter and Saturn, is closed.

He is seventy-seven, a marquis, a peer, and the most decorated scientist in Europe, and he has spent thirty years learning that the way to survive a change of regime is to owe nothing to the one going out. Francois Arago, twenty-seven years his junior and one of the Sunday men at Arcueil in the good years, is by now the loudest liberal in French science and does not forgive him. No primary record of the protest has been found.

stops.name: 108 rue du Bac, Paris: the death
stops.date_confidence: Date attested by MacTutor, which also records that the Academie cancelled its meeting as an exceptional mark of respect and that his seat stood empty for months until Puissant's election. The address is attested by fr.wikipedia 'Rue du Bac', whose entry for No. 108 says that Laplace lived there, as a plaque records, and not that he died there; the death address is the pool's synthesis. The Academie des sciences cancels its meeting, which it does not do, and leaves his chair unfilled for months afterwards. Alessandro Volta dies the same day at Como. Then his physician Francois Magendie takes the brain out of the skull. It is kept for years and shown at last in a travelling anatomical museum in Britain, where it is reported to be below the average size, and no catalogue listing it has ever been found.

stops.name: Beaumont-en-Auge, the return to the birthplace
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged and not resolved, and it is the largest single factual gap in the research pool. fr.wikipedia's infobox for Laplace lists three resting places: Pere-Lachaise until 1878, the cemetery of Beaumont-en-Auge from 1878 to 1888, and Saint-Julien-de-Mailloc from 1888. en.wikipedia and napoleon-empire.org compress this into one 1888 transfer from Pere Lachaise straight to Saint-Julien-de-Mailloc, and the pool's chronology lens followed the simpler account while its afterlife lens caught the three-stage version. The ten years at Beaumont are recorded here because one source carries them and no source denies them. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: Fifty-one years after the funeral the remains are lifted out of Pere Lachaise and carried back into Normandy, to the cemetery of the town where he was born and schooled, in sight of the priory that taught him Latin and a hundred and twenty-nine years after the parish register recorded his baptism. They lie there ten years. This middle grave appears in one source only. The standard account in English moves him in a single step from Paris to the family tomb and does not mention the town at all.
suggested_refs: The cemetery of Beaumont-en-Auge, Calvados, resting place 1878-1888 per fr.wikipedia's infobox

stops.name: Saint-Julien-de-Mailloc, the Colbert-Laplace tomb
stops.date_confidence: The 1888 transfer is attested by fr.wikipedia. The tomb known as the tombeau des Colbert-Laplace, the sixteenth-century chapelle Notre-Dame-de-la-Delivrande beside it, the Chateau de Mailloc (seventeenth century, inscrit MH, four mallets on a tower), and Laplace's purchase of the chateau in 1813 are all from fr.wikipedia 'Saint-Julien-de-Mailloc', which also gives the coordinates 49 deg 04 min 51 sec N, 0 deg 19 min 08 sec E used here; the research pool's geography lens gave 49.0333, 0.4167, about nine kilometres off, and contradicted its own afterlife lens. He is laid there in 1888 and has not been moved since. In 1925 the chateau burns, and the family papers burn with it: letters, drafts, accounts, whatever the household still held of him. The house belongs then to his great-great-grandson, the Comte de Colbert-Laplace.

stops.name: Beaumont-en-Auge, the bronze with Galileo and Newton
stops.date_confidence: Attested by fr.wikipedia 'Beaumont-en-Auge': the bronze is by Robert Delandre, inaugurated on 3 July 1932 by Marshal Louis Franchet d'Esperey, with medallion portraits of Galileo and Newton on the pedestal. Newton's view that the solar system requires periodic divine correction is stated in the Opticks, Query 31, and is the position Laplace's stability work displaced.

Set into the pedestal are two medallion portraits, Galileo and Newton: the man who took the heavens away from Aristotle, and the man who gave them a law and then wrote that the law would need correcting from time to time by God. The stability proofs of the cider merchant's son are why he stands above the two of them. Below the statue the priory church he was schooled beside is now the parish church of the town.
